n: Why compassion and accountability belong together

blocks.x: There comes a moment in leadership when the theories, models and carefully constructed frameworks offer surprisingly little comfort. You find yourself sitting opposite another human being, knowing that the decision you are about to make may have a profound effect on their life, their livelihood or their future. This is why Leadership is never easy.

Perhaps someone has failed to meet an important professional standard. Perhaps a valued colleague is struggling personally, and their difficulties are beginning to affect others. Or perhaps your organisation is facing financial pressures, and you must make decisions that will disappoint people who have given years of loyal service. You may have to speak to someone who you know are full of trauma, whatever it is. As a Leader it is your job to soften and relieve that trauma. These are not hypothetical dilemmas for those who have spent their careers leading people. They are the uncomfortable realities of leadership, and they rarely come with straightforward answers.

Over many years of working in the Prison Service, including serving as a Prison Governor, I came to understand something that has shaped my thinking ever since: compassion and accountability are not competing leadership principles. Indeed, I would argue that the most effective leadership often emerges precisely where the two meet. Yet across organisations, we continue to encounter the assumption that compassionate leaders are somehow less demanding, less decisive or less willing to confront poor performance.
I believe the opposite can be true.
Compassion is not the absence of difficult decisions

Prisons are extraordinary places in which to learn about leadership. They bring together people from very different backgrounds, often under considerable pressure, within environments where safety, security, human dignity and organisational responsibility must coexist. Decisions carry consequences, sometimes significant ones, for staff, prisoners, families and the wider community.

Throughout my career which spanned thirty-five years, I encountered situations in which people needed understanding and support, but where professional standards and organisational responsibilities could not simply be set aside. There were occasions when individuals were experiencing considerable personal difficulties, yet their behaviour or performance still required challenge.

Leading within a prison brings with it an extraordinary weight of responsibility. Imagine being accountable for several hundred prisoners, each with their own complex needs, circumstances and vulnerabilities, alongside several hundred members of staff, each bringing their own experiences, expectations and challenges. Every day presents decisions that can have profound consequences for individuals, the wider organisation and the communities we serve. In such an environment, leadership demands far more than operational competence. It requires consistency, authenticity, sound judgement and a genuine commitment to treating people with fairness, dignity and compassion. Decisions must be carefully considered, sometimes made under considerable pressure, and always guided by a determination to achieve the best possible outcome, even when the choices available are difficult or imperfect. The challenge is not simply to make the right decision, but to make it for the right reasons, in the right way, while never losing sight of the people whose lives may be affected.

Compassion did not remove my responsibility to act. It influenced how I approached that responsibility. It required me to listen, to understand circumstances, to recognise the complexity of human behaviour and to consider the consequences of my decisions. But it also required me to be clear about expectations, honest about shortcomings and prepared to take difficult action when necessary.

This understanding is consistent with the work of Professor Michael West and colleagues at The King's Fund. Their research on compassionate leadership identifies four interconnected behaviours: attending, understanding, empathising and helping.

What matters here is that compassion is not simply a feeling of sympathy towards another person. It involves making a genuine effort to understand their circumstances and then taking thoughtful action. For leaders, that action may involve providing support, removing barriers, addressing unfairness or creating opportunities for improvement. But it may also involve a difficult conversation, a clear expectation or an uncomfortable decision.
Compassion is not an alternative to responsibility. It is a way of exercising responsibility with humanity.
When kindness becomes avoidance

One of the more uncomfortable truths about Leadership is that our desire to be liked, or simply to avoid causing distress, can sometimes prevent us from doing what is necessary and often appropriate. I have seen leaders postpone difficult conversations because they genuinely cared about the person involved. They recognised that someone was struggling and did not want to make matters worse.

The intention was understandable. The consequences were not always helpful. When poor performance is left unaddressed, the individual concerned may be deprived of the opportunity to improve. Colleagues may become frustrated at having to compensate for shortcomings, and the organisation can gradually develop a culture in which expectations are negotiable and difficult issues remain unresolved.

The irony is that avoiding discomfort in the short term can create considerably greater distress in the longer term. Leadership author Kim Scott addresses this tension in her work on Radical Candor, arguing for an approach that combines two principles: "Care Personally" and "Challenge Directly".

It is a deceptively simple proposition, but one that captures an important leadership responsibility. Caring about someone does not mean withholding honest feedback. Equally, challenging someone does not require us to abandon respect, kindness or dignity. The challenge is to do both, and that is often considerably more difficult than choosing one or the other.
Accountability without humanity carries its own dangers
Of course, there is another side to this argument.

Some organisations have developed cultures in which accountability is understood almost exclusively through targets, performance indicators, compliance and consequences. These things have their place. Organisations must deliver, public services must remain accountable, and leaders have legitimate responsibilities to maintain standards. But accountability becomes dangerous when it is reduced to the exercise of authority rather than the development of responsibility. When people fear humiliation, blame or disproportionate consequences, they may become reluctant to acknowledge mistakes, admit uncertainty or challenge decisions.

Problems are concealed rather than explored. People become skilled at demonstrating compliance rather than exercising professional judgement. Professor Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety is particularly relevant here. Her work challenges the assumption that creating an environment in which people feel safe to speak up means lowering expectations or accepting poor performance.

Psychological safety is about creating an environment in which people feel confident to speak openly, acknowledge mistakes, ask questions and challenge established thinking without fear of humiliation, criticism or punishment. It does not mean that people are exempt from accountability. For me, that distinction is fundamental.

An organisation in which people feel unable to speak honestly is unlikely to learn effectively from its mistakes. But an organisation in which people feel supported without being held to appropriate standards will face difficulties of a different kind. Effective leadership requires us to establish both the confidence to speak openly and the expectation that people will take responsibility for their work.
The uncomfortable questions leaders should ask themselves

My postgraduate research at the University of Cambridge explored humanitarian leadership within prisons. It gave me an opportunity to examine academically many of the questions I had encountered throughout my professional career.

One conviction became increasingly important to me: Leadership should not be judged solely by the achievement of organisational objectives, but also by the way those objectives are pursued and the human consequences of the decisions made along the way. This is not an argument against performance. It is an argument for recognising that performance, productivity and humanity are deeply connected.

And it raises some difficult questions for those of us entrusted with leadership responsibilities. When someone makes a mistake, is our first instinct to establish blame or to understand what happened? When an individual is underperforming, do we consider whether they have received the clarity, support, resources and development necessary to succeed?

When we make an unpopular decision, do we take time to explain our reasoning and acknowledge its consequences? Are we prepared to challenge unacceptable behaviour even when the person involved is someone we respect, value or personally like? And perhaps most importantly, would the people we lead describe our leadership in the same terms that we use to describe ourselves?
That last question deserves particular attention. Because the culture we believe we have created is not necessarily the culture that others experience.
Leadership is experienced, not announced
Most organisations can produce an impressive list of values. Let's say -
Respect. Integrity. Compassion. Accountability. Inclusion.

They appear in strategic plans, recruitment materials, induction programmes and on office walls. Yet their real meaning is established through the everyday experiences of the people who work within those organisations. People notice how leaders behave when things go wrong.

They notice whether mistakes are treated as opportunities for learning or occasions for humiliation. They notice whether senior colleagues are held to the same standards as everyone else, whether concerns are genuinely heard and whether compassion remains visible when difficult decisions must be made.

Michael West's work on organisational culture reinforces the importance of leadership behaviour in shaping the environments in which people work. What leaders pay attention to, reward, challenge and consistently demonstrate communicates what an organisation truly values. This is why I have always been cautious about organisations that describe themselves as compassionate without being prepared to examine how that compassion is experienced in practice.
A statement of values is an aspiration. Culture is what people encounter when they come to work. And the distance between those two things can sometimes be considerable.
The courage to acknowledge our own shortcomings

There is another dimension to accountability that deserves greater attention: the accountability leaders owe to themselves and to those they lead. Leadership experience does not make us infallible. I have made decisions throughout my career that, with the benefit of hindsight, I would approach differently today. There have been occasions when I could have listened more carefully, communicated more effectively or recognised sooner the difficulties someone was experiencing.

I do not regard acknowledging those shortcomings as a weakness. I regard it as an essential part of developing as a leader. The most impressive leaders I have encountered are not necessarily those who appear to have all the answers. They are often the people who remain curious, who are prepared to reconsider their assumptions and who recognise that holding others accountable carries an equally important obligation to examine their own conduct.

There is something deeply contradictory about demanding openness, honesty and responsibility from colleagues while refusing to demonstrate those qualities ourselves. Compassionate leadership must therefore include the capacity for self-reflection, humility and a willingness to learn. Not because these qualities make leaders appear more approachable, but because they make leadership more credible.
Bringing compassion and accountability together

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, our philosophy is built around a simple commitment: helping people to lead well in hard places. Those hard places are not confined to prisons or other demanding operational environments. They exist in charities facing funding pressures, businesses navigating uncertainty, public services experiencing increasing demands and leadership teams struggling to reconcile organisational priorities with the needs of their people.

They exist wherever leaders must make decisions that affect others, particularly when there is no obvious or comfortable solution. Our belief is that compassion and accountability should reinforce one another rather than compete. Compassion encourages us to understand people, their circumstances and the consequences of our decisions. Accountability ensures that responsibilities are honoured, standards are maintained and commitments are taken seriously.

Together, they create the conditions in which people can feel respected, supported, challenged and trusted. This approach does not eliminate difficult conversations, unpopular decisions or the inevitable tensions of organisational life. Nor does it guarantee that leaders will always get things right. But it does offer a more thoughtful, responsible and humane way of exercising leadership.
And in organisations where people increasingly expect their leaders to demonstrate both competence and humanity, I believe that matters enormously.
A final reflection

I would invite every leader reading this article to think about the last genuinely difficult decision they made. Not simply whether the decision was correct, justified or necessary, but how it was experienced by the people affected. Were they listened to? Were they treated with dignity? Did they understand the reasons behind the decision? And were you prepared to examine your own assumptions before reaching a conclusion?
These questions will not always produce comfortable answers, but perhaps that is precisely why they matter.
Because leading well is not about choosing between compassion and accountability. It is about having the courage, judgement and humanity to practise both, especially when doing so is difficult.

refs: Edmondson, A. C. (2019). The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. Wiley.
Scott, K. (2017). Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity. St. Martin's Press.
West, M., Eckert, R., Collins, B., & Chowla, R. (2017). Caring to Change: How Compassionate Leadership Can Stimulate Innovation in Health Care. The King's Fund.

n: The culture you think you have may not be the culture your people experience

blocks.x: There is a question I believe every senior leader should ask themselves, although I suspect many would find the answer uncomfortable.
What if the organisation you believe you are leading is not the organisation your people experience every day?

You may believe your organisation is open, supportive and compassionate. You may be confident that people feel listened to, that colleagues are encouraged to challenge decisions and that your leadership team operates with integrity and mutual respect.

Your employee surveys may even suggest that things are generally going well. But what happens when we look beneath the surface? What happens when we speak to the people who rarely contribute during meetings, who have stopped raising concerns or who have quietly concluded that challenging established thinking is simply not worth the effort?

What might they tell us about the organisation? And perhaps more importantly, would we be prepared to listen? Throughout my leadership career, I have become increasingly convinced that one of the greatest risks facing senior leaders is not necessarily a poor organisational culture. It is believing that the culture is healthier than it actually is.
Culture is not what we say it is

Most organisations can describe their values with considerable confidence. They have carefully developed mission statements, strategic objectives, behavioural frameworks and commitments to respect, inclusion and accountability. There is nothing inherently wrong with these things. They provide direction and communicate important expectations. But they do not, by themselves, create culture.

Edgar Schein, one of the most influential scholars of organisational culture, distinguished between the visible features of an organisation, its stated values and the deeper assumptions that shape how people actually behave. This distinction is fundamental.

An organisation may publicly celebrate openness while employees privately believe that questioning senior leaders will damage their careers, we know this happens, most people do. It may promote compassion while allowing unacceptable behaviour from influential individuals to go unchallenged. It may describe itself as collaborative while rewarding competition, individual achievement and the protection of departmental interests.

The organisation's stated values may be entirely sincere, but the culture experienced by its people tells a different story. In my experience, the most revealing evidence of organisational culture is often found not in what leaders say, but in what people have learned is safe, rewarded, tolerated or best avoided.
The view from the top is rarely the whole picture

Senior leaders occupy a distinctive position within organisations. They have access to information, influence decisions and often experience the organisation through carefully structured meetings, reports and performance discussions.

Their colleagues may be respectful, cooperative and apparently enthusiastic. But those interactions do not necessarily reveal how the organisation functions elsewhere. Indeed, the more senior we become, the more important it is to recognise that our position can influence what people are willing to tell us.

People may soften criticism, avoid difficult subjects or provide reassurance because they believe that is what senior leaders want to hear. This is not always deliberate dishonesty, sometimes it is simply a rational response to organisational experience.

Chris Argyris explored the ways in which individuals and organisations develop defensive routines that protect people from embarrassment or threat but can also prevent genuine learning. Over time, these routines can become embedded in organisational life. Difficult issues are discussed privately rather than openly. Problems are presented in ways that minimise concern and often meetings produce agreement without genuine challenge.

And furthermore, senior leaders may interpret the absence of disagreement as evidence of confidence and alignment. But silence is not necessarily agreement. Sometimes it is simply what it is, silence.
What people learn from our behaviour
I spent much of my professional life leading in prisons, where organisational culture has profound implications for safety, performance, staff wellbeing and the treatment of people in custody.

In such environments, leaders cannot afford to assume that what is happening at senior management level accurately reflects the experience of those working on the front line. A policy may appear clear in a management meeting but be interpreted very differently in practice. A decision may seem reasonable from an organisational perspective but create unforeseen pressures for the people expected to implement it.

A leadership team may believe that staff feel supported while colleagues elsewhere experience something quite different. Of course, these challenges are not unique to prisons. They are found in hospitals, schools, charities, social enterprises, commercial businesses and public services, and so many more.

People learn what matters to an organisation by observing how leaders behave, particularly when circumstances become difficult. They notice whose opinions carry weight, which behaviours are challenged, who receives recognition and what happens when someone makes a mistake. They also notice the gap between what leaders promise and what they consistently deliver. And over time, those observations become powerful influences on organisational culture.
Psychological safety and the willingness to speak

Professor Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety provides an important perspective on this issue. Psychological safety concerns the shared belief that people can take interpersonal risks, such as asking questions, acknowledging mistakes, raising concerns or challenging established thinking, without fear of humiliation or inappropriate punishment. It is sometimes misunderstood as creating an environment in which everyone feels comfortable all the time. That is not the point.

Healthy organisations still experience disagreement, challenge, difficult conversations and accountability. The difference is that people are not discouraged from contributing because they fear the personal consequences of speaking honestly.

Consider what happens when an employee raises a concern during a meeting. Does the leader respond with curiosity, or immediately become defensive? Is the concern explored, or quickly explained away? Does the individual feel their contribution has been taken seriously, even when the organisation ultimately decides not to act upon it?

These seemingly small interactions matter. They communicate whether openness is genuinely valued or merely encouraged in principle. And they influence whether others will be willing to speak up next time.
The danger of comfortable leadership teams

There is another risk that deserves attention. Leadership teams can become so familiar with one another, and so comfortable with their established ways of working, that they gradually lose the capacity to challenge their own assumptions.

Meetings become predictable and the same individuals dominate discussions. Difficult issues are deferred. Decisions are made without sufficient consideration of alternative perspectives. The team may continue to function efficiently, but efficiency should not be confused with effectiveness.

A leadership team that rarely disagrees may be exceptionally well aligned. Or it may have developed a culture in which disagreement is discouraged. How would we know the difference? This is where genuine reflection becomes important.

Leaders need opportunities to step outside their operational responsibilities and examine not simply what their organisation is achieving, but how they are working together and what their behaviour is communicating to others. Sometimes the most valuable question a leadership team can ask is not whether it has delivered its objectives, it is whether its own behaviour is helping or hindering the organisation it leads.
Listening is not the same as hearing

Many organisations are understandably proud of their employee engagement arrangements. They conduct surveys, hold staff forums, establish working groups and encourage feedback. These mechanisms can be extremely valuable.

But collecting feedback is not the same as understanding it and understanding it is not the same as acting upon it. A survey may reveal that employees lack confidence in senior leadership. The temptation may be to improve communication, arrange additional briefings or explain organisational decisions more clearly and sometimes that will be appropriate.

But what if the underlying issue is not communication? What if people understand the decisions perfectly well but do not trust the way those decisions are made? Or what if they have repeatedly raised concerns without seeing meaningful change? Additionally what if they believe that senior leaders are more interested in defending existing arrangements than understanding their experience?

In those circumstances, more communication may achieve very little. The organisation needs to understand what lies beneath the feedback. That requires curiosity, humility and a willingness to hear things we may not particularly want to hear. It also requires us to resist the temptation to interpret every uncomfortable finding as a misunderstanding that needs correcting. Sometimes the feedback is telling us something important about ourselves.
The importance of holding up the mirror

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, we believe organisational development should begin with understanding rather than assumption. Before designing leadership programmes, introducing new initiatives or attempting to change workplace culture, it is worth asking whether the organisation genuinely understands its current position.

These questions form part of the thinking behind our Reflection & Culture Survey and our Leadership Diagnostic Assessments. Their purpose is not simply to produce a report or another set of organisational statistics. It is to create opportunities for honest reflection, meaningful conversations and practical improvement.

A well-designed diagnostic process should help leaders identify strengths worth protecting, challenges that need attention and assumptions that may require reconsideration. It should also provide a starting point for collective ownership of change. Because understanding organisational culture is not the responsibility of the HR department alone. It is a fundamental leadership responsibility.
What happens after the feedback matters most

There is, however, an important caution. Inviting people to share their experiences creates an expectation that their contributions will be taken seriously. If employees are encouraged to speak honestly but subsequently see no acknowledgement, explanation or action, the process can undermine rather than strengthen trust.

But not every concern can be resolved and not every suggestion can be implemented. And sometimes leaders must make decisions that remain unpopular despite genuine consultation. But people should understand what has been heard, what will happen next and why certain decisions have been made. They should also have opportunities to contribute to the development of solutions.

Culture is not transformed by a survey, it changes through the decisions, behaviours and relationships that follow. That is why organisational diagnostics should be viewed as the beginning of a conversation rather than the conclusion of an exercise.
The courage to see what others see

Perhaps one of the most demanding aspects of senior leadership is accepting that our intentions do not always match the experiences of those we lead. We may genuinely believe that we are approachable, yet others may find us intimidating. We may believe that we encourage challenge, yet colleagues may have learned that disagreement is unwelcome and we may consider ourselves compassionate, yet people may experience our decisions as distant or impersonal.

Acknowledging these possibilities does not mean that we have failed as leaders. It means recognising that leadership is experienced through the perceptions, relationships and circumstances of other people, and those experiences deserve our attention.

The most effective leaders I have encountered have not been those who insisted that their organisations were healthy, supportive or high performing. They have been those who were prepared to find out whether that was actually true. They understood that credibility comes not from claiming to have created the right culture, but from demonstrating a genuine willingness to understand, challenge and improve it.
A final reflection
If I were to ask the people closest to you whether your organisation has a healthy leadership culture, what would they say?
Now consider a more difficult question.

What would the people who rarely speak in meetings, who work furthest from senior leadership or who have previously raised uncomfortable concerns say? Would their answers be the same? And if they were different, would you genuinely want to know why?

The culture we think we have is not necessarily the culture our people experience. The responsibility of leadership is to have the courage to discover the difference and the commitment to do something about it.

refs: How do people experience leadership at different levels? Do employees believe they can speak openly?
Are expectations clear and consistently applied?
Do stated values align with everyday behaviour?
Are senior leaders working collectively towards a shared purpose, or are organisational pressures pulling them in different directions?
And crucially, where are the differences between leadership intentions and employee experiences?
Argyris, C. (1990). Overcoming Organisational Defences: Facilitating Organizational Learning. Allyn & Bacon.
Edmondson, A. C. (2019). The Fearless Organisation: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. Wiley.
Schein, E. H. (2010). Organizational Culture and Leadership (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.

n: Why good managers don't automatically become great Leaders

blocks.x: There is a familiar pattern in organisations that I suspect many of us will recognise. Someone performs exceptionally well in their role. They are knowledgeable, dependable, hardworking and consistently deliver results. They understand the operation, solve problems and earn the confidence of senior colleagues.

Eventually, an opportunity arises for promotion. Their success makes them an obvious candidate and eventually they are appointed to a more senior position, given greater responsibility and expected to lead a team. And then something interesting happens.

The qualities that made them so effective in their previous role do not necessarily equip them for the responsibilities of their new one. They may understand the operation better than anyone else, but struggle to delegate. They may be highly capable decision-makers yet find difficult conversations uncomfortable. They may have an exceptional work ethic but inadvertently create a culture in which everyone feels they must work at the same relentless pace.

They have been promoted because they were good at their job. But nobody has necessarily helped them understand that their job has fundamentally changed. I believe this is one of the most common, and least adequately addressed challenges in organisational leadership.
The promotion that changes everything

During my career in the Prison Service, I worked alongside many exceptionally capable operational managers. They understood complex environments, made decisions under pressure and demonstrated remarkable commitment to their responsibilities.

Some progressed naturally into outstanding senior leaders and others found the transition considerably more difficult. Not because they lacked intelligence, commitment or integrity, but because leading people requires capabilities that are not always developed through operational experience alone.

A manager may be accustomed to solving problems personally. As their responsibilities increase, however, their effectiveness becomes increasingly dependent upon helping others develop the confidence, judgement and capability to solve problems themselves, and that is a significant transition.

It requires a shift from being the person with the answers to becoming someone who can ask better questions. From directing activity to developing capability, from measuring personal achievement to understanding collective performance. And from managing the immediate demands of an operation to considering the longer-term consequences of decisions, relationships and organisational culture.
These changes do not happen automatically when someone receives a new job title. They require deliberate development, reflection and, often, considerable personal adjustment.
The difference between managing and leading

Management and leadership are sometimes presented as competing disciplines, with management associated with systems and processes and leadership associated with inspiration and vision. I have never found that distinction entirely satisfactory, organisations need both.

Effective management provides structure, clarity, coordination and accountability. Without these, even the most compelling vision can become little more than an aspiration. Leadership, however, brings an additional responsibility: helping people understand purpose, navigate uncertainty, develop their capabilities and contribute to something beyond their immediate tasks.

The two are interconnected, and effective senior leaders must often exercise both. The difficulty arises when organisations assume that excellence in one automatically guarantees excellence in the other.

Ronald Heifetz's work on adaptive leadership is particularly relevant here. Heifetz distinguishes between technical problems, which can often be addressed through existing expertise and established procedures, and adaptive challenges, which require people to learn, reconsider assumptions and change established ways of working.

This distinction matters because many managers are promoted precisely because they have demonstrated an ability to solve technical and operational problems. Yet their new responsibilities may increasingly involve challenges for which there is no straightforward technical solution.
These challenges cannot simply be resolved through instructions, policies or performance indicators, they require leadership.
When expertise becomes an obstacle
One of the paradoxes of leadership development is that the expertise which helps someone achieve promotion can sometimes become an obstacle to their subsequent effectiveness.

Imagine a newly appointed senior manager who has spent years being recognised for their ability to resolve operational difficulties. Their instinct, when presented with a problem, is to take control, they intervene, provide answers and make decisions.

Initially, this may appear highly effective. But over time, colleagues can become dependent upon their intervention. Managers stop exercising their own judgement, difficult decisions are escalated unnecessarily, and the senior leader becomes increasingly overwhelmed. The problem is not a lack of capability; it is that the leader has continued to rely upon the behaviours that made them successful in a different role.

I have seen variations of this throughout my career, and I suspect many experienced leaders will recognise something of themselves in it. Learning to delegate is not simply about distributing tasks. It is about trusting others, accepting that they may approach problems differently and resisting the temptation to intervene whenever something is not done exactly as we would have done it ourselves.

That can be particularly challenging for leaders who have built their professional identity around being competent, knowledgeable and dependable. But unless we create opportunities for others to develop, we risk becoming the very obstacle that prevents our teams from progressing.
The "Human Dimension" of leadership
Technical expertise may help someone understand what needs to be achieved however it does not necessarily help them understand how to bring people with them.
Daniel Goleman's influential work on emotional intelligence brought greater attention to the importance of self-awareness, self-regulation, empathy and interpersonal relationships in leadership.

Although emotional intelligence should not be treated as a complete explanation of leadership effectiveness, it offers an important perspective. Leaders need to recognise how their own emotions, behaviours and communication influence others. They need to understand that people do not always respond to pressure, uncertainty or challenge in the same way. And they need to appreciate that the impact of their behaviour may be very different from their intentions.

A leader who believes they are demonstrating urgency may be experienced as impatient. Someone who considers themselves decisive may be perceived as dismissive, and a manager who prides themselves on maintaining high standards may unintentionally create an environment in which colleagues are reluctant to admit mistakes.

None of these outcomes necessarily reflects poor intentions, but leadership cannot be judged by intention alone. It must also be understood through the experience of those being led. This is why self-awareness matters so much. Without it, even highly capable individuals can struggle to recognise the consequences of their own behaviour.
The danger of promoting people and then leaving them to cope

There is a responsibility here that extends beyond the individual leader. Organisations frequently invest considerable time in recruitment and promotion processes, assessing candidates against competencies, reviewing performance and testing their suitability for more senior roles. Yet once the appointment has been made, meaningful leadership development can become surprisingly limited.

The individual receives a new title, greater responsibility and perhaps an induction programme, and then they are expected to deliver. We would rarely expect someone to undertake a technically demanding professional responsibility without appropriate preparation. Why then, do we sometimes assume that people can develop the complex interpersonal and strategic capabilities of leadership simply through experience?

Experience is undoubtedly important, but experience without reflection does not necessarily produce learning. People can spend years repeating the same behaviours, reinforcing the same assumptions and making similar mistakes without fundamentally developing their leadership capability.

Research by David Day and colleagues on leadership development emphasises that developing leaders involves more than acquiring knowledge or attending training programmes. It also concerns the development of individual capabilities, relationships and the capacity to operate effectively within wider organisational systems.
This distinction is important; Leadership development should not be treated as an occasional event. It should be understood as an ongoing process of learning, application, feedback and reflection.
Coaching is not a remedy for failure

One of the misconceptions I would particularly like to challenge is the assumption that leadership coaching is primarily intended for people who are struggling. Of course, coaching can be valuable when someone is experiencing difficulties. But some of the greatest benefits arise when capable, ambitious and committed leaders are given the opportunity to examine how they think, behave and influence others.

Good coaching creates space for conversations that are often absent from the pressures of organisational life. It allows leaders to explore their assumptions, recognise patterns in their behaviour and consider alternative approaches to familiar challenges. It also encourages them to confront questions that may otherwise remain unasked.

These are not necessarily comfortable questions, but they can be profoundly developmental. At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, we believe coaching should be both supportive and challenging. It should create the conditions for honest reflection while maintaining a clear focus on personal responsibility, professional growth and improved organisational outcomes.

The purpose is not to provide leaders with a collection of fashionable techniques. It is to help them develop the judgement, confidence and self-awareness necessary to lead effectively in the circumstances they actually face.
Developing leaders who develop others

There is another dimension to this discussion that organisations sometimes overlook. The effectiveness of a leader should not be measured solely by what they personally achieve. It should also be judged by the capability, confidence and independence they develop in others.

A leader who consistently delivers results through personal intervention may appear highly successful. But what happens when that person is absent, does the team continue to function effectively? And are colleagues confident in exercising judgement? Or, can emerging leaders make difficult decisions without constantly seeking reassurance? Furthermore, has the organisation become dependent upon one individual's knowledge, authority and availability?

These questions reveal something important about leadership maturity. Developing others requires patience, trust and a willingness to relinquish control. It means allowing colleagues to learn through experience while ensuring that appropriate support and accountability remain in place. It also means recognising that leadership is not simply something exercised by people occupying senior positions.

Leadership capability can and should be developed throughout an organisation. When people are encouraged to think critically, take responsibility and support one another, the organisation becomes more resilient. And that is a far more sustainable achievement than the success of any single individual.
The importance of reflective practice

Looking back on my own leadership career, I recognise that some of my most important learning did not come from formal training or academic study. It came from difficult experiences, challenging relationships, mistakes, honest feedback and occasions when I was forced to reconsider assumptions I had previously taken for granted.

My postgraduate studies at the University of Cambridge subsequently gave me an opportunity to examine those experiences through a more structured academic lens. What became increasingly clear was that professional experience and academic understanding are most valuable when they inform one another.

Theory can challenge the assumptions we develop through practice, experience can expose the limitations of theory, and reflection creates the opportunity to learn from both. For organisations, this suggests that leadership development should involve more than teaching people what effective leadership looks like. It should create opportunities for individuals to examine their own behaviour, apply new learning and receive meaningful feedback. Without that process, development risks becoming something people attend rather than something they experience.
From capable managers to effective leaders

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, we work from the belief that leadership capability can be developed, strengthened and refined throughout a person's career. We also recognise that effective development must begin with an understanding of the individual.

Two managers may occupy similar positions and face comparable responsibilities yet require very different forms of support. One may need to develop confidence in challenging difficult behaviour; another may need to learn to delegate more effectively. A third may be technically exceptional but struggle to build relationships or create a shared sense of purpose.

This is why our approach combines leadership coaching, diagnostic assessment, reflective practice and practical development opportunities. We want to help individuals understand not simply what they need to do differently, but why their existing approaches may no longer be serving them or the people they lead. Because leadership development is not about turning everyone into the same type of leader. It is about helping people become more effective, thoughtful and accountable versions of themselves.
A final reflection
If you lead an organisation, I encourage you to think about the people you have promoted into management and leadership positions over recent years.

There is nothing wrong with promoting people who demonstrate technical excellence, commitment and operational competence. Indeed, these qualities can provide an excellent foundation for leadership. But they are a starting point, not a guarantee.

Being good at managing work does not automatically mean we are good at leading people. Recognising that distinction, and investing in the development needed to bridge it, may be one of the most important responsibilities any organisation has.

refs: How do you rebuild trust in a divided team?
How do you help experienced colleagues adapt to an uncertain future?
How do you challenge an organisational culture that has become defensive or resistant to change?
Why do I find delegation so difficult?
Why do certain individuals or situations provoke a disproportionate response?
Am I genuinely listening to colleagues, or simply waiting for an opportunity to explain my own position?
What might my team say about my leadership if I were not in the room?
Why were they selected?
Was it because they demonstrated the potential to inspire, develop and lead others?
Or was it primarily because they were exceptionally good at the work they were already doing?
And once appointed, what meaningful support did they receive to help them make that transition?

n: The conversations Leaders avoid are often the ones that matter most

blocks.x: One of the more uncomfortable realities of leadership is that we sometimes know exactly what needs to be addressed but find ourselves reluctant to address it. An individual's performance may have deteriorated, relationships within a team may have become strained, or behaviour that was initially dismissed as an isolated incident may have developed into something more concerning. The signs are often apparent, and yet the conversation that might begin to resolve the situation is repeatedly postponed.

Throughout my career in the Prison Service, including my years as a Prison Governor, I encountered situations in which difficult conversations were unavoidable. They were not always about misconduct, poor performance or organisational failure. Sometimes they involved supporting colleagues through personal difficulties while maintaining professional expectations. On other occasions, they required challenging established practices, confronting uncomfortable truths or explaining decisions that people understandably found difficult to accept. What these experiences taught me was that the quality of leadership is often revealed not through the conversations we find easy, but through our willingness and ability to engage constructively with those we would rather avoid.

It is important however, to understand why avoidance occurs. Leaders do not necessarily postpone difficult conversations because they lack courage or professional competence. Many genuinely care about their colleagues and are concerned about causing distress, damaging relationships or making an already difficult situation worse. Others may lack confidence in their ability to manage disagreement, particularly when emotions are running high. These concerns are understandable, but they do not remove the responsibility to act when circumstances require it.
The organisational cost of avoidance

When a leader decides not to address a difficult issue, the consequences rarely remain confined to the individuals directly involved. Consider a situation in which a capable but challenging member of staff consistently behaves in ways that undermine colleagues. Their technical competence may be valued, their contribution to organisational performance may be significant, and their manager may be reluctant to risk losing them. Over time, however, other colleagues begin to question why behaviour that contradicts the organisation's stated values is apparently tolerated.

The resulting damage can be considerable. Trust in leadership may diminish, previously engaged colleagues may withdraw, and resentment can develop among those who feel that expectations are being applied inconsistently. What initially appeared to be a relatively contained management issue becomes a broader question about organisational fairness, accountability and culture.

Research by Professor Amy Edmondson on psychological safety provides an important perspective. Her work demonstrates the importance of environments in which people can raise concerns, acknowledge mistakes and challenge established thinking without fear of humiliation or inappropriate interpersonal consequences. When leaders consistently avoid addressing difficult behaviour, they risk communicating that maintaining superficial harmony matters more than creating an environment in which people can contribute honestly and confidently.

There is also a danger that avoidance becomes embedded within organisational culture. If senior leaders repeatedly defer difficult decisions or tolerate behaviours they would otherwise condemn, managers elsewhere may conclude that challenging uncomfortable issues is neither expected nor particularly welcome. Over time, this can produce organisations in which problems are widely recognised but rarely discussed openly, and where the appearance of agreement becomes more important than genuine understanding.
Compassion does not mean avoiding discomfort

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, we place considerable emphasis on Compassionate Leadership, but I am conscious that compassion is sometimes misunderstood as an obligation to protect people from discomfort. In reality, Compassionate Leadership can require considerable personal courage, particularly when a leader must challenge someone they respect, value or genuinely care about.

Kim Scott's work on Radical Candor offers a useful perspective through her emphasis on caring personally while challenging directly. The underlying principle is that honest feedback and genuine concern for another person's wellbeing are not mutually exclusive. Indeed, withholding important feedback because we fear causing discomfort may ultimately disadvantage the very person we are trying to protect.

The distinction lies in how we approach the conversation. There is a considerable difference between confronting someone with the intention of asserting authority and engaging with them because their behaviour, performance or circumstances require thoughtful attention. The former can produce defensiveness and resentment, while the latter creates an opportunity for understanding, accountability and improvement. Neither approach guarantees a comfortable discussion, but the intention, preparation and conduct of the leader can significantly influence what follows.

My experience has also taught me that compassion requires us to recognise the circumstances surrounding an individual's behaviour without automatically excusing its consequences. Someone may be experiencing genuine personal difficulties, yet their responsibilities to colleagues and the organisation remain important. The challenge is to understand what support may be appropriate while remaining clear about the standards and expectations that must be maintained.
This balance is rarely achieved through rigid scripts or predetermined responses. It requires judgement, curiosity and the willingness to listen carefully before deciding what should happen next.
The importance of how we communicate

Difficult conversations often become more challenging because leaders approach them with conclusions already formed. We may have gathered information, discussed concerns with colleagues and developed a clear view of what has happened before the individual concerned has had an opportunity to explain their perspective. Although preparation is essential, there is a danger that it becomes a process of reinforcing our existing assumptions rather than remaining open to new information.

Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton and Sheila Heen explore this problem in their book Difficult Conversations, drawing attention to the different interpretations, emotions and questions of identity that frequently sit beneath disagreements. Their work encourages us to recognise that individuals may experience the same situation very differently, and that productive conversations require an effort to understand those differences rather than simply establish whose interpretation is correct.

For leaders, this means entering difficult discussions with both clarity and curiosity. We should be clear about the issue requiring attention, the impact it is having and the expectations that must be met. Equally, we should be prepared to listen to information that challenges our initial understanding. A conversation that begins with an assumption of wrongdoing or deliberate underperformance may overlook circumstances that are essential to reaching a fair and proportionate conclusion.

This does not mean avoiding difficult messages or allowing discussions to become so open-ended that accountability disappears. Effective conversations require a balance between understanding the individual's perspective and maintaining clarity about responsibilities, decisions and next steps. People should leave knowing what has been discussed, what is expected and what support or action will follow.

The ability to achieve this balance is an important leadership capability, yet one that organisations do not always develop sufficiently. Managers may receive extensive training in operational processes, policies and performance systems while having relatively limited opportunities to practise the interpersonal skills required when those systems involve real people experiencing real difficulties.
Leadership responsibility extends beyond the conversation

It would be misleading to suggest that every difficult conversation produces a positive outcome. Sometimes individuals disagree with the concerns raised, relationships remain strained or formal action becomes necessary. Leaders may have to make decisions that are entirely appropriate but nevertheless distressing for those affected. Compassionate Leadership does not eliminate these possibilities, nor should it be judged solely by whether everyone leaves a conversation feeling satisfied.

What matters is whether the leader has approached the situation fairly, thoughtfully and with an appropriate sense of responsibility. Were the concerns explained clearly? Was the individual given a genuine opportunity to respond? Were relevant circumstances considered, and were expectations communicated without unnecessary humiliation or hostility? These questions are particularly important when the outcome cannot be negotiated or when the leader must exercise formal authority.

There is also a responsibility to consider what happens afterwards. A difficult conversation should not simply become an isolated event that allows the leader to feel that an issue has been addressed. Depending upon the circumstances, meaningful follow-up may involve additional support, agreed improvements, further discussions or a clear process for reviewing progress. Where wider organisational concerns have emerged, leaders may also need to examine whether existing systems, expectations or cultural behaviours have contributed to the problem.

This is where reflective leadership becomes particularly important. We should be willing to consider not only whether the conversation was conducted appropriately, but also whether our own actions, assumptions or previous reluctance to intervene played a part in allowing the situation to develop.
Developing the confidence to lead difficult conversations

I have long believed that leadership development is most valuable when it addresses the realities that people encounter in their professional lives. Difficult conversations provide a particularly useful example because they bring together so many of the capabilities that effective leadership requires: emotional awareness, professional judgement, clear communication, fairness, accountability and the ability to understand another person's perspective.

These capabilities cannot be developed solely by reading a framework or attending a presentation. They require opportunities for practice, reflection, constructive challenge and feedback. Leaders need space to examine why particular conversations make them uncomfortable, how their own communication style influences others and what they might do differently when faced with similar circumstances in the future.

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, this understanding informs our approach to executive coaching, leadership development and practical workshops. We recognise that leaders operate in different organisational contexts, often under significant pressure, and that effective development must take account of those realities. Our purpose is not to provide a universal script for difficult conversations, but to help leaders develop the confidence, judgement and interpersonal capability to approach them more effectively.

There is a broader organisational responsibility here too. If we expect managers to address challenging behaviour, support colleagues through difficult circumstances and maintain professional standards, we must ensure they have access to appropriate development and support. Simply expecting people to acquire these capabilities through experience can leave them unnecessarily exposed and can create avoidable difficulties for the teams they lead.
A final reflection

When I reflect upon the most challenging periods of my leadership career, I am reminded that difficult conversations were rarely made easier by postponing them. There were occasions when additional information, careful preparation or a more appropriate moment were genuinely necessary, but these should not be confused with avoidance. Knowing when to act, when to listen and when to allow time for reflection is itself an exercise of leadership judgement.

I would encourage leaders to consider whether there is a conversation within their organisation that has remained unresolved for longer than it should. It may concern performance, behaviour, trust, professional relationships or an uncomfortable issue that everyone recognises but nobody has been prepared to confront. Whatever the circumstances, it is worth considering not simply why the conversation feels difficult, but what the continuing absence of that conversation may be costing others.

Ultimately, compassionate and accountable leadership requires more than good intentions. It demands the willingness to engage with uncomfortable realities, to treat people with dignity and fairness, and to accept responsibility for addressing issues that cannot simply be wished away. The conversations we avoid are often the ones that matter most because they reveal whether our leadership values are genuinely reflected in our behaviour.

refs: Edmondson, A. C. (2019). The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. Wiley.
Scott, K. (2017). Radical Candor: Be a Kick-Ass Boss Without Losing Your Humanity. St. Martin's Press.
Stone, D., Patton, B., & Heen, S. (1999). Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most. Viking.

n: When Leadership teams lose their way: Rebuilding purpose, trust and direction

blocks.x: It is entirely possible for an organisation to be busy, productive and apparently successful while gradually losing sight of where it is going. Senior managers attend meetings, operational targets are monitored, financial reports are scrutinised and decisions are made about the immediate challenges facing the organisation. Individually, those involved may be highly capable, experienced and committed to their responsibilities. Yet beneath this activity, something important can begin to disappear: a shared understanding of purpose, collective responsibility and a clear sense of strategic direction.

This rarely happens suddenly. More often, it develops gradually as organisations grow, demands increase and senior leaders become increasingly absorbed in their own areas of responsibility. Meetings that once provided opportunities for strategic discussion become dominated by operational updates, immediate problems and competing priorities. Important questions about the organisation's future are repeatedly deferred because there is always something more urgent requiring attention.

Over time, the leadership team may continue to function efficiently without necessarily functioning collectively. Individuals remain accountable for their departments, services or professional responsibilities, but the wider organisation begins to experience the consequences of fragmented leadership. Decisions become disconnected, priorities compete for attention and colleagues further down the organisation struggle to understand how their work contributes to a coherent direction.

Throughout my career, I have worked in environments where the demands of operational leadership were considerable. Prisons are particularly challenging in this respect because immediate responsibilities relating to safety, security, staffing and organisational performance cannot simply be postponed. Yet these pressures also reinforced an important lesson: senior leaders must retain the capacity to look beyond the demands of the present and consider the organisation they are collectively responsible for creating. This is not always easy, but it is fundamental to effective leadership.
A leadership team is more than a collection of senior managers

One of the assumptions I have increasingly questioned is that bringing capable individuals together automatically creates an effective leadership team. Organisations often invest considerable effort in recruiting talented executives and senior managers, each possessing expertise within their own professional discipline. What receives less attention is whether those individuals have developed the relationships, shared understanding and collective accountability necessary to lead the organisation as a whole.

A finance director may understandably prioritise financial sustainability, while an operational director concentrates on service delivery and a people director focuses on workforce development. These perspectives are all essential, but difficulties arise when they become competing interests rather than complementary contributions to a shared organisational purpose.

Richard Hackman's research on team effectiveness provides a useful perspective. His work emphasises that effective teams require more than talented individuals; they need a compelling direction, an appropriate structure and conditions that support meaningful collaboration. Applied to senior leadership, this challenges the assumption that collective effectiveness will emerge naturally from individual competence.

The question is not simply whether each director is performing well within their own responsibilities. It is whether the leadership team is exercising effective collective judgement about the future of the organisation, the choices it must make and the consequences of those choices for its people.

I have encountered senior teams where individual members were exceptionally capable, yet their collective effectiveness was constrained by competing priorities, insufficient challenge or an absence of shared direction. The difficulty was not necessarily a lack of commitment. It was that the team had not developed a sufficiently strong understanding of what collective leadership required.
When operational pressures displace strategic thinking

Every organisation must respond to immediate demands. Financial pressures, staffing difficulties, regulatory requirements, changing customer expectations and unexpected events all require leadership attention. In complex environments, these pressures can consume considerable time and energy, particularly when resources are limited.

The danger emerges when responding to immediate problems becomes the dominant purpose of the senior leadership team. Meetings become increasingly reactive, with substantial attention devoted to reviewing what has happened rather than considering what needs to happen next. Leaders may become highly skilled at managing organisational pressures without creating sufficient space to examine their underlying causes.

Henry Mintzberg's work on managerial roles and organisational strategy reminds us that management is often fragmented, demanding and shaped by competing pressures. His research offers a useful challenge to idealised descriptions of senior leadership in which strategic thinking appears to take place separately from the complexities of everyday organisational life.

In practice, leaders must deliberately create the conditions for strategic reflection. It is unlikely to happen consistently if it depends upon finding spare time after operational responsibilities have been completed.

This does not mean that senior teams should become detached from operational reality. Indeed, strategies developed without a meaningful understanding of the organisation's people, services and practical constraints are unlikely to succeed. The challenge is to connect immediate operational decisions with a longer-term sense of purpose, ensuring that today's pressures do not continually determine tomorrow's direction.

A useful question for any senior leadership team is whether its meetings are primarily concerned with managing the organisation as it currently exists or shaping the organisation it needs to become. Both responsibilities matter, but an imbalance between them can gradually weaken strategic leadership.
Trust, challenge and collective responsibility

Even where a leadership team has established a clear strategic direction, its effectiveness depends upon the quality of relationships between its members. Trust is particularly important, although it is sometimes misunderstood as the absence of disagreement or the maintenance of harmonious working relationships.

In my experience, effective leadership teams are not necessarily those in which everyone agrees. They are teams in which people are sufficiently confident in their relationships to challenge assumptions, question decisions and express concerns without those contributions being interpreted as personal opposition.

Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety is relevant here because it highlights the importance of environments in which individuals can speak openly, acknowledge uncertainty and contribute different perspectives. Within senior leadership teams, this is particularly significant because the consequences of unchallenged assumptions can extend throughout an organisation.

A leadership team that rarely experiences disagreement may be exceptionally well aligned, but it may also have developed habits that discourage constructive challenge. Individuals may avoid questioning colleagues because they wish to preserve relationships, protect departmental interests or avoid appearing disloyal. Over time, the absence of meaningful challenge can create an illusion of collective agreement while important differences remain unresolved.

Collective responsibility also requires leaders to recognise that their obligations extend beyond the interests of their own departments or professional disciplines. A decision that benefits one service may create difficulties elsewhere, while an initiative that appears operationally attractive may place unsustainable demands upon the workforce or the organisation's finances.

The purpose of a senior leadership team is not simply to negotiate between competing departmental interests. It is to exercise collective judgement about what is right for the organisation as a whole. That responsibility requires both trust and accountability. Leaders must be willing to support collective decisions while remaining prepared to challenge the assumptions upon which those decisions are based.
Reconnecting strategy with people

One of the greatest risks associated with organisational growth and change is that strategic decisions become increasingly distant from the people expected to implement them. Senior leaders may develop ambitious plans, establish new priorities and introduce revised performance arrangements, yet fail to create a meaningful understanding of what these changes will require from colleagues throughout the organisation.

A strategy may be intellectually coherent and financially credible while remaining poorly understood by the workforce. Employees may recognise that changes are taking place without understanding their purpose, how decisions have been reached or what contribution they are expected to make. This matters because organisational strategy is not delivered by documents. It is delivered through the decisions, relationships and everyday activities of people.

John Kotter's work on organisational change emphasises the importance of establishing direction, building commitment and enabling people to contribute to change. Although no single model can capture the full complexity of organisational development, the underlying lesson remains valuable: leaders cannot assume that announcing a strategy is equivalent to creating collective ownership of it.

Throughout my professional life, I have become increasingly convinced that people are more likely to contribute meaningfully when they understand not only what is expected of them, but why their contribution matters. This requires communication, certainly, but it also requires genuine engagement and a willingness to listen to those whose experiences may challenge senior leadership assumptions.

For organisations experiencing growth, this responsibility becomes particularly important. Structures, systems and relationships that were effective when an organisation was smaller may no longer be sufficient as its responsibilities expand. Senior leaders must consider how to preserve the organisation's values and sense of purpose while developing the governance, infrastructure and leadership capacity required for its future.

Growth should not simply be measured by increasing income, expanding services or employing more people. It should also prompt reflection upon whether the organisation's leadership arrangements, culture and systems are developing at a pace that enables that growth to remain sustainable.
Creating space to hold up the mirror

There are occasions when senior leadership teams benefit from stepping outside their normal routines and examining their collective effectiveness with greater honesty. This can be particularly valuable following periods of rapid growth, significant organisational change, leadership transitions or prolonged operational pressure.

The purpose of such reflection should not simply be to identify weaknesses or produce another set of improvement actions. It should create an opportunity for leaders to consider whether they share a common understanding of organisational purpose, whether their strategic priorities remain appropriate and whether their own behaviours are supporting the culture they wish to develop.

These discussions are not always comfortable. They may reveal differences in ambition, unresolved tensions or assumptions that have remained unchallenged for considerable periods. Yet such discoveries can be valuable if leaders approach them with curiosity, mutual respect and a willingness to accept collective responsibility.

At EmpathyWorks Leadership Consultancy, this understanding informs our approach to strategic facilitation, organisational diagnostics and leadership team development. We believe that meaningful organisational improvement begins with an honest assessment of the present, a shared understanding of the future and a practical commitment to bridging the distance between them.

Our role is not to arrive with predetermined answers or impose a standard model of organisational effectiveness. It is to help leadership teams examine their circumstances, challenge their assumptions and develop a clearer understanding of the choices available to them.

Importantly, we also recognise that strategic reflection must lead to practical action. A successful leadership workshop should not be judged simply by the quality of discussion on the day, but by whether the organisation subsequently makes meaningful progress towards the priorities it has identified.
That requires clear ownership, realistic timescales, appropriate measures of progress and a commitment to reviewing what has changed.
Leadership must look beyond the immediate horizon

The most effective senior leaders I have encountered understand that their responsibility extends beyond maintaining current organisational performance. They recognise that they are also shaping the conditions in which others will work, develop and lead in the future.

This involves making decisions about organisational capability, succession, culture and long-term sustainability, often while managing considerable immediate pressures. It requires an appreciation that today's decisions may have consequences that extend well beyond the tenure of the individuals making them.

For chief executives and senior leadership teams, this creates a particular obligation to consider not simply whether the organisation is performing adequately today, but whether it is becoming stronger, more resilient and better equipped to fulfil its purpose tomorrow.

It also requires the humility to recognise when established ways of working are no longer sufficient. Organisations change, expectations evolve and approaches that once delivered success may gradually become barriers to further progress. Leadership teams must therefore remain willing to examine themselves with the same seriousness that they apply to organisational performance.

This can be difficult, particularly for experienced leaders who have invested considerable effort in building the organisation and may understandably feel protective of what has been achieved. Nevertheless, genuine stewardship requires us to recognise that protecting an organisation's purpose sometimes means being prepared to change the way it operates.
A final reflection

If you are part of a senior leadership team, I would encourage you to consider when you last spent meaningful time discussing the future of your organisation without allowing immediate operational demands to dominate the conversation.

Do you share a clear understanding of where the organisation is going and why? Are your strategic priorities sufficiently focused to guide difficult decisions, or have they become an extensive collection of ambitions that compete for attention? Do colleagues feel able to challenge one another constructively, and are you genuinely exercising collective responsibility for the organisation rather than primarily representing your individual areas of expertise?

Perhaps most importantly, if you asked people throughout your organisation to describe its future direction, would their understanding reflect the intentions of the senior leadership team? These are not questions that can be answered adequately through a single meeting or a carefully prepared strategy document. They require ongoing reflection, honest discussion and a willingness to examine the relationship between leadership intentions and organisational experience.

Effective leadership teams do more than manage organisational activity. They establish direction, create the conditions for collective achievement and accept responsibility for the long-term health of the organisations entrusted to them. When that shared purpose becomes obscured by operational pressures, competing priorities or weakened relationships, the task of leadership is to recognise what has been lost and work collectively to rebuild it.

Ultimately, the strength of a leadership team is not determined simply by the experience or capability of the individuals around the table, but by their ability to think, decide and act together in the interests of the organisation and the people who depend upon it.

Hackman, J. R. (2002). Leading Teams: Setting the Stage for Great Performances. Harvard Business School Press.
Kotter, J. P. (1996). Leading Change. Harvard Business School Press.
Mintzberg, H. (1973). The Nature of Managerial Work. Harper & Row.
